Prevention: Avoid intercropping with host crops e.g. potato, eggplant, capsicum, tobacco.
Avoid overhead irrigation as it spreads the disease.
Avoid field operations during wet weather.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops e.g. maize, cabbage, onion, or beans for one year.
Do not grow potatoes or tomatoes on land that has had this disease for at least 5 years.
Disinfect all farm tools in chlorine-based products for at least 5 minutes.
Pruning knives should be disinfected after pruning every plant.
Monitoring: Look out for seedlings with small, water-soaked lesions on foliage, stunting, wilting, later death.
Progressive wilting leaves that curl upwards, turn brown, wither & later dry up while attached to the stem.
Infected stems split, resulting in open cankers.
Pith is reddish-brown, grainy (mealy) or pitted.
Raised lesions with white margins (“bird’s eye” spot) on fruits.
Take action when one plant is affected.
Direct Control: Carefully uproot and destroy infected plants by burying to not spread infected soil.
Apply a dry mulch to reduce the spread of the disease.
Spray with bronopol- and chrysophanol-based products.
Restrictions: When using a pesticide always wear appropriate personal protective equipment.
Follow the instructions on the product label on dosage, maximum applications, PHI, Re
entry interval, and disposal of pesticide waste.
No synthetic chemicals are registered against bacterial canker in tomatoes.
However, the following pesticides have been found to control bacterial diseases in other crops.
However, effective copper-based products can be used.
Spray with copper oxychloride- based products.
